title: Divided votes: with a donor’s side, and with everyone else’s
question: On divided roll calls, did a member vote the way a party wanted more often when that party was already in the member’s donor circle?
finding: No more than chance: across three sets of divided roll calls, 42 member-and-party pairs had the party already in the member’s donor circle, and the member voted the party’s way in 31 of them (73.8%), where voting like the other members on the same roll calls would have given about 32 (7,848 of 10,000 shuffles reach 31 or more). Land-use matters: of 71 divided roll calls (2015 to 2026, one per appeal), 18 involve an organization whose wanted outcome is on record (it filed the appeal, or a lobbyist’s client asked for support or opposition by file number), giving 251 member-and-party pairs, 10 of them (from 2 roll calls: Perkins Coie LLP; all lobbyists’ clients seeking passage) with the party already in the member’s donor circle. The member voted the party’s way in 8 of those (80.0%), against 64.9% of the 37 pairs with the same kind of party outside the circle: within what chance would produce; the other members on the same roll calls voted that way 80.0% of the time. Money files: of 3,483 final Board votes on disk (2015 to 2026), 123 were divided and 45 of those name an outside organization, which wants the file passed, giving 533 member-and-party pairs, 14 of them (from 7 roll calls: Accenture, Pacific Gas and Electric, Planned Parenthood Northern California and others; all organizations the file names as its counterparty) with the party already in the member’s donor circle. The member voted the party’s way in 11 of those (78.6%), against 82.7% of the 519 pairs with the same kind of party outside the circle: within what chance would produce; the other members on the same roll calls voted that way 87.3% of the time. Other lobbied measures that are not land-use matters: 21 divided final votes, 9 with a lobbyist’s client whose side is on record, giving 96 member-and-party pairs, 18 of them (from 5 roll calls: San Francisco Chamber of Commerce, San Francisco Deputy Sheriff's Association, San Francisco Travel Association; all lobbyists’ clients seeking defeat and lobbyists’ clients seeking passage) with the party already in the member’s donor circle. The member voted the party’s way in 12 of those (66.7%), against 68.0% of the 78 pairs with the same kind of party outside the circle: within what chance would produce; the other members on the same roll calls voted that way 54.0% of the time. 1 of the 14 roll calls with a donor-circle party was decided by one or two votes (0 of the 2 land-use ones). No organization that filed an appeal was in the donor circle of a member who voted on it (204 pairs). Member by member, 1 of 33 has enough pairs on both sides to test; 1 differs by more than chance (Shamann Walton, who voted with donor-circle parties less often than with others).
how: Only roll calls with at least one aye and one no are used, because a unanimous vote says nothing about any one member. Three sets are kept apart. Land-use matters, as before: Board and committee roll calls on appeals and lobbied land-use files, where sibling files of one appeal that print the same vote are counted once. A party is an organization named as appellant (the text after “on behalf of”) or the client of a lobbyist whose reported contacts cite the file number and ask for support, approval or opposition. For an appeal the party’s side is “uphold”: an aye on a motion to reverse or disapprove, or a no on a motion to affirm or approve. For other files it is passage or defeat. The votes analysis counts 81 divided full-Board roll calls of every kind on land-use matters; here motions to continue or table are left out, committee roll calls are included and the sibling files of one appeal count once. Money files: the final Board passage roll call (the last roll call on ADOPTED, APPROVED, PASSED ON FIRST READING or FINALLY PASSED, as the shared roll-call reader defines it) of each contract, grant agreement, lease, property, loan or business-settlement file whose title names an outside organization; that organization is taken to want the file passed, so an aye is a vote its way. Files by which the City accepts a grant or gift are left out, because the money flows to the City, and so are counterparties that are public bodies or private individuals; appropriations name no counterparty. Other lobbied measures: the final Board passage roll call of a file that is neither a land-use matter nor in the money set, where a lobbyist’s reported contacts cite the file number and ask for support or opposition. A party is in a member’s donor circle when the organization, or a donor naming it as employer, gave to the member’s candidate committee, to a ballot committee carrying the member’s name or to a committee others formed to support the member, at any date before the vote; 2 pairs in which everything given had been returned before the vote are not counted as donor-circle pairs. Donor-circle pairs are compared only with pairs involving the same kind of party in the same set (an appellant, a client seeking passage, a client seeking defeat, a counterparty), with Fisher’s exact test; the pairs from one roll call are not independent of each other, so that test overstates certainty. The column “Within the same roll calls” therefore makes the stricter comparison: each roll call’s votes are kept as they were, and which of its voting members count as the donor-circle members is shuffled ten thousand times. The member rows pool the three sets and compare each member’s donor-circle pairs with that member’s other pairs of the same kinds.
limits: Being connected is not being corrupt. Member-by-member roll calls are now on disk for money files and for measures a lobbyist cited by file number, from 2015, as well as for land-use matters; ordinances that no lobbyist cited by number are still not covered. For 332 roll calls the Clerk’s vote page says “by the following vote” and lists no member, 306 of them dated 2016-04-13 to 2016-07-26; 315 were read instead from the vote lines in the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and 17 remain without member votes and are counted nowhere here. Most money files are routine and pass without dissent, so the divided ones are a small and unusual subset, and in most of them a single member voted no: nearly every member votes for nearly every money file, donor or not. Donors give to members who already share their view, so voting a donor’s way is expected without any exchange, and a donor naming an employer says where the donor works, not that the employer gave. With 33 members in the table, one or two would cross the 5% line by chance alone. Counterparties are read by machine from file titles and matched by exact name, so links are undercounted. Project sponsors are rarely named in titles, so the applicant’s side of an appeal is mostly missing here. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
